utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Buenos dias, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could have continued in Spanish, Madam Registrar, but it's not one of the languages of the Tribunal so I stopped it after saying good morning. For the record all the accused are here. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, and Sarapa and Mr. Petrusic, would always be behind the column, so I couldn't notice his absence too. The Prosecution same composition as yesterday. The witness is already in the courtroom. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. We are going to proceed with Mr. Josse's cross-examination, hoping that he will finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The issue, Sir Rupert, that I wish to begin with this morning relates to a matter that we touched on yesterday, and I said that I would return to today, and that is the distinction between NATO and UNPROFOR in relation to your command activities. Were you the NATO commander in Bosnia in, shall we say, July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a NATO commander in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent did you have a say over the deployment of purely NATO rather than UNPROFOR troops and/or missions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to be coordinated with me, and since NATO was operating in the sky as opposed to on the ground, this was usually a matter of time rather than place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've already explained to us about the dual key procedure, so I'm not going to go through that again. All the ground troops from, shall we say, United Kingdom and France were UNPROFOR troops under your command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were placed by their nation under the UN command, then they came under my command, yes, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the airplanes in the sky were all under NATO control or --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must be careful of the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The air space was controlled by NATO but not all the airplanes were commanded by NATO. So there were helicopters from various -- helicopter units from various nations that were part of the UN force and there were some UN contracted - I think was the relationship - airplanes from the Ukraine, but their movements and so forth were under the NATO control as they moved around in that air space and that had to be the case because of the no-fly zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Josse. Following this series of questions, I think some clarification is called for. General, you said there wasn't a NATO commander in Bosnia. Was there a NATO command or a NATO and a NATO commander anywhere in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think there was. The forces of NATO were commanded from Naples and Vicenza. They were -- where are we, in the middle of 1995? Yes. They were doing the air operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they had no base in Bosnia or anywhere else in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In relation to this, I would like to examine one sentence in your book "The Utility of Force," 6D186 and it's page 345. Whilst that is being done, let me just ask you one question. The only aircraft involved in combat activity were under the command of NATO, not UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by that you mean dropping bombs or firing cannon, those were NATO airplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why might the expression combat activity cover --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you were carrying troops, that might be considered as a combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. So far as this is concerned, page 345, about ten lines down --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see which is it the left or right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's in vision at the moment.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's about ten lines down and the sentence that begins, "Technically." I'll read it very slowly, yes, the icon is on it: "Technically, both NATO and the UN were in confrontation with the Bosnian Serbs, but NATO was focused only on the Bosnian Serbs whilst UNPROFOR was dealing with all sides to the conflict and their respective positions." What does the word "focused" mean there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense that if you've shined the light on it you focus the light on that thing. In this case NATO was focused on the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were NATO, as far as you were concerned, in confrontation with either of the other two parties to the war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Their activities were all focused on the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And whose decision was that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally, if you go back, it's both the NATO council, North Atlantic Council, and then where necessary it is then covered by Security Council resolutions, and it's the safe area, the exclusion zone -- sorry, the no-fly zones and the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I just want to be clear about this. You are not suggesting that you were not involved -- sorry it's a double negative -- you accept that you were involved to a degree in NATO decision-making; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in at the level of North Atlantic Council and so forth. As I said, my business was that of coordination and so forth at this stage in the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The rapid reaction force, what was its relationship to NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rapid reaction force was a UN force. It was -- it came from NATO nations or nations who were in NATO, and it came -- it was forming up during this period of June and July, and was a UN force once its elements had been passed to the command of the United Nations by the countries who found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we look at page 355 of this book, please? This is a sub-chapter that's headed, "We fight so as to preserve the force" and at the bottom of 354, which I'm not going to read out, you deal with the aftermath of the hostage taking of May 1995, how the idea of the rapid reaction force gathered momentum, and then going on to 355 at the top, you describe how it was going to be formed, and then about five lines down, it says, "The force was not to adopt the UN blue helmets or paint their vehicles white. It was an unmarked UN force. This was fine by me, they were to fight, and I did not want them to look like the UN. "I particularly wanted the guns. In comparison with aircraft, guns with appropriate target locating and fire control systems apply fire as accurately, can maintain the fire for longer, are not weather-dependent, and would be under my command. They could, in the right quantities, and deployment, defeat the Bosnian Serb artillery." So in your mind, this was a force with which to fight Mladic. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To fight whoever was getting in my way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Bosnian Serb artillery was under the command of Mladic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the ones who were shelling me at the time, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a few minutes time but the -- let me go on. "If this RRF were to be used successfully, its employment had to come as a surprise and yet its deployment was going to be in full view. It seemed to me, therefore, that I should avoid being seen as the commander of the force, it should be thought of as being under the hand of others, NATO, the nations, or even the UNHQ in Zagreb. "If Mladic had thought the force was under my hand, especially after the bombing in May, he would have made sure he had potential hostages at hand to seize and guns in range of vulnerable UN positions. I decided to share this understanding with no one and played my cards accordingly." No one means no one? Not a soul?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did discuss it with anybody. No. That was my own idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so the idea was what, to lull Mladic or the VRS into a false sense of security?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a sense of security. It was, as I've said there, to conceal that this force was under my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were fairly open about the deployment of this force with both the Croat and Bosniak leaders, would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with everybody else. There was no -- it was -- it was generally known. It was in all the press. It was published -- there was a Security Council resolution about it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the problem you faced, among other things, was a certain amount of reticence on the part of Dr. Izetbegovic, the Croat leadership, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, we had to deploy it through Dalmatia and into Bosnia, and the other parties were suspicious of it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By the other parties, you mean?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Federation as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your mind, as the extract I have just read out makes clear, this rapid reaction force was only ever going to be deployed against one party in the dispute. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most probable party was the Bosnian Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the force, as I think you told us in your evidence-in-chief, consisted of British, French and some Dutch troops; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the -- was the makeup. I don't think there were any other nations involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of the commanders, who was the British contingent in the command structure in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battle group was commanded by a Colonel Cook, if I recall correctly. The artillery was a Colonel Applegate, and the air mobile brigade that was held down on the coast was a Brigadier Brims, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you ask you about the involvement first of all of an officer called Pennyfeather? I'm not sure his rank.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Major General.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They deployed later, as a -- as a separate headquarters, to stand -- after the London Conference, to connect better the actions of the rapid reaction force with those of NATO, so that there was a headquarters that pulled those two organisations together that was in -- in Bosnia, and would act as my reserve headquarters should I be -- my headquarters is in Sarajevo, should that be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about a Major General Wilcox?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Wilcox is the Chief of Staff of the headquarters called a NATO headquarters, the Allied Command Europe Reaction Corps is I think is its title. Hang on a minute. I think it's just reaction corps, ARC is the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what in a sentence, if you can, was their role?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure at the time that they had had a formal role. They were certainly the headquarters that, if -- that came in to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1996 or very late 1995, and -- but depending where we are in the time scale, I don't think certainly not in June that they had a -- anything other than a watching brief in NATO parlance, and I just don't know what their -- they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, last name in this list, a General Michael Walker?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the commander of that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of that corps?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wilcox is his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the 7th of November, at page 17653 of the transcript of this trial, you were being cross-examined by my learned friend representing General Miletic, and she asked you the following: "Did you ever think of taking stronger action against the Bosnian side to prevent such attacks from happening?" And you asked for clarification of that. And she said, "Did you take any measures at all after you received such reports?" You then said, "When we had a particular case, we would pursue it, and in many cases these would be protested and so forth in much the same procedure as was carried out with, to the Bosnian Serbs, when other things happened from that side." Question: "But on various cases, force was used against the Serbs? Did you ever think of using force against the Bosnian side?" Answer as follows, and this is what I'm going to need to ask you concentrate on at the moment: "There was no case where that I can recall in my time when the Bosnians attacked my forces, so I had no cause to use force in defence of myself or my forces." Did you mean what you said in that answer?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to think of a case when there was an attack on my forces that -- at all, let alone one that one considered using force in response to it, but I can't think of one immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's see if I can help you a little bit over the next few minutes. First, and some would perhaps say foremost, relates to a time where I accept that you, Sir Rupert, were on leave, and that was the unfortunate killing of the Dutch soldier, Private Renssen, on the 8th of July of 1995 in Srebrenica by armed Bosniak men. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. And yes, I think it was done by the Bosnians, and if I -- now you're reminding me, I think the Dutch forces withdrawing through the Bosnian line in those -- in that set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That may be right. I want to put -- I think the best thing is to put this on the ELMO, Your Honour, because we are not sure of the number and we can sort this out later, but I've got one unmarked copy here. It's a letter, Sir Rupert, from General Janvier to General Delic, dealing with this incident, again relating to a time when you were on leave. I'm not going to read it all out, but we see that he begins by saying that he deeply shocked to learn of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army hostile action against an UNPROFOR armoured personnel carrier on the 8th of July, and he expressions his deepest indignation with regard to what he describes as the murder of a Dutch soldier in the area of Srebrenica. This second paragraph describes the incident, third paragraph the same, the fourth paragraph says, and I'll go a little slower, "There is no question that the fire came from your soldiers." General Janvier describes it as a flagrant and totally unnecessary action against my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've moved this. There we go. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you would like to read?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was wanting to see what date he sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you'd like to read the whole letter, feel free, but I think that's the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just looking for the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was this discussed at Geneva?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, that the man had been killed was discussed or reported at Geneva. I don't think we had -- I don't recall any of those facts as laid out in that -- in that letter, being explained at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that I clearly had to show you this in order to jog your memory about this, about the incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The next item in relation to the same issue is best dealt with by us having a look at 1D44 in e-court, please. This, Sir Rupert, is a witness statement from a Lieutenant in the Dutch Brigade, and we are only going to look at a very small portion of it. I can see my learned friends looking through our list. These aren't on our list. This is a result of very recent work done yesterday as a result of cross-examination by my learned friend Madam Fauveau, and so we have not disclosed the use of these documents. It's a decision that we literally made overnight, Your Honour. That's what happens in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the bottom of that page, Lieutenant Koster says, "At the end of January 1995, the Muslim fighters wanted us to keep out of a certain part of the enclave." And I think this was the part that was called the Bandera Triangle, stopping there. But anyway I'll go on. "Major Franken and eight soldiers of the reconnaissance platoon endeavoured to enter this area in order to enforce the condition of freedom of movement. When they did so, they were taken hostage. I believe that Zulfo, a subordinate commander in the Muslim forces, was responsible for this hostage-taking. I never saw this Zulfo. He was one of Naser Oric's commanders. I later heard that there was an internal power struggle between these two men. When this happened, Major Boering and van Alphen went to negotiate and were also taken hostage by BiH fighters. In total, about 75 to 100 men were taken hostage. These men were taken hostage when they were on stand-by near what is known as the Bandera Triangle. This was in the western part of the enclave. So according to Lieutenant Koster, this was in late January after you had taken up your command. Do you have any recollection of this going on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't and I'm not sure that I necessarily was there then. But if I had been, it was right on the time I was taking over and I don't recall a briefing of this issue. I can -- I knew that things were not easy and relationships were not good in Srebrenica. It's one of the reasons I'd been trying to get there in the subsequent weeks, but I don't remember that particular case laid out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's try again. 6D132, please. This is an UNPROFOR sit-rep for the 17th of July of 1995. And it appears to relate to events in Gorazde at that time. I'll read it in a moment. Were you aware that there were difficulties in Gorazde at the time of the Srebrenica-Zepa events?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look at this, then. According to the information received from BritBat through the SAT phone call in the night from 15 to 16 July 1995, the Bosnians took as hostage UKRCOY --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ukrainian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ukrainian command Lieutenant-Colonel Bakolic [phoen] and demanded to give them up all weapons, equipment, and ammunition and threatened to kill commander in an hour when negotiations failed. 60 men from Special Forces and 100 from regular troops penetrated the Ukrainian enclosure and confiscated all weapons, military equipment, vehicles, ammo, and medicines. BiH supported their actions by fire at the Ukranian compound, only four vehicles left and I'm not going to read out the rest." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you clearly didn't remember it a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't count that as the same heading, if that's what you -- I can give you another example of that and it happened even later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and help you by answering what I think is your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had authorities to use military force in self defence. I had it over -- for the exclusion zones at this stage in the -- that year. The case of the soldier killed by the Bosnians in Srebrenica, the case -- this case, it -- by the time you knew about them, by the time it was over, you were no longer within the parameters of any of those authorities to use force, even if you'd wanted to, you were outside that particular set of boundaries, and I thought you were asking me about the questions of where one might have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you want to explain why this was outside the boundary of your power?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because by the time that is over, anyone knew about it, you were no longer in a position to defend the Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And these boundaries or perimeters were defined by whom, the Security Council, by UNPROFOR itself, explain?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of engagement in terms of self-defence and so forth came down, if not directly from the Security Council, certainly from UN headquarters, through the Zagreb, and each country had slightly -- each contributing nation had slightly different interpretations of those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind you now know where I'm going, perhaps you would tell us other examples that come to your mind, in particular ones that occurred later than this incident --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I recall is -- was in Bihac. Whether it's October-November, I'm not sure, but it was later in the year, when the Bangladesh contingent had a similar experience to the Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why couldn't you do anything there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: For exactly the same reason. It was over and done with by the time one had discovered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of any similar type of events in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- it occurred, much of what you've just described there is happening in Zepa as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I could show you some documents but Avdo Palic, does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the, if I recall correctly, the commander of the Bosnian forces in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's sometimes called the Zepa Brigade, that's right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he threatened to kill the Ukrainians, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. In an UNPROFOR document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR documents also reveal that Palic's men attacked the Ukrainian compound?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but if that's what it says, then they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's just have a quick look at 6D92, please. This is the 20th of July, ABiH is firing at Ukrainian company --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- with heavy machine-guns, Bosnian soldiers have thrown several grenades into the Ukrainian enclose. Ukrainian personnel took a defensive position but didn't respond yet. Situation is extremely critical. And your answer presumably would be that this had all passed by such time as you could have done anything and therefore you weren't mandated to try and take control of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do the documents show what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not the ones that I have to hand. I'm more than happy to receive any help from my learned friends in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can spend a lot of time showing General Smith the same situation reports which show threats and attacks by the VRS forces, attacks by the BiH forces, specific death threats from VRS forces if NATO were used, and we can spend hours doing that. I'm happy to go up and get those documents and bring them down, but I'm not sure it's going to be productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not the point. That's not the point of this at all. The point of this arises from the answer that this witness gave in cross-examination earlier, and indeed I think the question that General Smith just asked is what happened immediately after this, as to whether he would have been in a position to do anything about it. I'm confessing that I don't know the answer off the top of my head. So what my learned friend said is really not the point at all in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed, perfectly legitimate question and I don't think one correlates to the other, Mr. Thayer. As Mr. Josse said, this is the aftermath or sequel to the question which Madam Fauveau had asked and which the general had answered. Yes, Mr. Josse. We are at a point where the General Smith was about to possibly tell us what happened after this. Are you in a position to -- you asked whether there were documents --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if the document went on or anything like that to explain what happened next. I -- I would expect that Sector Sarajevo would have started to get on to their opposite numbers in the Bosnian army, possibly telling my headquarters and my headquarters doing the same, to ask what the hell was going on and to stop it. I don't know whether it stopped or if those attempts were overtaken by events, but I know that in -- at about this time, there is this event in which, if not a lot of weapons, some weapons were taken from the Ukrainians by the defenders in Zepa. And I suspect this is the event, but I don't know. That's why I was asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am going to return to it a later in another guise, but I'm going to move on to another topic if I may at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have been asked a fair amount already about the failure of UNPROFOR to demilitarise the enclaves, and you would accept that UNPROFOR did not demilitarise the enclaves. Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Nor do I think it was -- that UNPROFOR's business, and I'm going back into the 1993-94 time, was not understood that they were the ones to demilitarise it, as in take all the weapons away and so forth. It was the understood, I think, as that they were there as it were, in an observer, in a -- role, rather than the executive role. But I quite agree it wasn't demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you accept that there were constant complaints from Bosnian-Serb military and political leaders that the enclave was not demilitarised? And when I say complaints, I mean complaints to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- they had been happening, yes. They were much -- they were-- much more before my time than in my time, but, yes, that had been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we could look at some documents where Karadzic complained to you and more particularly complaints were constantly made by the Bosnian Serb liaison officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Indic in meetings he had with his counterpart. You're probably aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quite agree. That was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question to you, Sir Rupert, is why did you do nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained. My -- the understanding originally was that this was a business between the parties to demilitarise: The UN was there in its standing-in-the-middle role and that was the situation that I was in in the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement when I arrived. And so the basis on which I was operating was that -- was from the situation when I arrived. I wasn't going to be able to turn the clock back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to examine with you the answer you gave to this question or a similar question when posed at the Dutch parliamentary inquiry, small extract of which you've already been asked about. It's 5D489. And it's page 680 at the bottom. At the bottom of the page, you in fact say, your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, which column, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Far right-hand column where the cursor is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your question is should we have forced the Bosnians to disarm? And the questioner clarifies that by saying, yes, that is right, but I do not mean that in moral terms. And this is your answer, and I should add that the questioner in his original question had made clear that this related to Srebrenica or Zepa. "Leave aside whether we should have done so or not. In principle terms and in practical terms, the argumentation for not taking that action was that we were impartial. We did not use force on either party because it was their agreement. It was up to them either to stick to it or not. Secondly, there were considerable other pressures to arm the Bosnians and to encourage them, from the United States" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we are moving to the next page, trying to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: --"and others. All of us faced another set of pressures, me, Zagreb, the Security Council, all whatever. The Serbs demanded that we should police the other side in this agreement. That was precisely how the Bosnian Serbs were approaching the UN. 'You, UN, have agreed to this and you agreed that they would be disarmed. Why do you not disarm them?' "However, the Bosnians were equally saying, 'You agreed to this and you were supposed to be able to supply us but you are not. Since you are not able to supply us, we will now go to fight for supplies.' "We entered this argument in which the UN finished up as a shield of one and a hostage to the other, to be punished by either of them because we were not doing what they wanted to do." Do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you relay that answer at the time to Karadzic and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not those terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were part of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of my problem. I'm now outside it to explaining it to somebody else. I'm explaining what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't mean -- perhaps, let me be clear. I don't mean the hostage and shield point. More the point that you were impartial and it was their agreement, and therefore really it was their problem. That's what it amounts to; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that when you got the situation such as you describe of people complaining about they hadn't disarmed, I cannot recall exactly how I answered the specific question at the time, and I would have certainly explained that the UN were in no position to do anything about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you make it clear that it was their agreement and therefore their problem? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember doing it in those terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because if it was their problem, they had to do something about it in the Bosniak case, they needed to get more supplies into the enclave. You say as much in your answer, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that's what they were doing. I don't remember telling them that that's what they should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so far as the VRS is concerned --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I certainly never told anybody to attack Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, no. But that's a logical consequence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not if I'm sitting in my position in the UN, not at all logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, isn't it -- if you're saying to these parties, you've got to police your own agreement, it's accepted -- let me finish, it's accepted that the Serbs, I beg your pardon, that the Bosniaks, are conducting military activity from within the enclave, the logical conclusion is that the VRS are going to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that logic, from my position as the UN commander, and I didn't tell them that they had to police their own agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me try again. Isn't that the logical conclusion to the answer you gave the Dutch parliamentary inquiry?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not, if an agreement isn't being followed through, it doesn't follow that you, the other party to the agreement, then carry out your own actions to put it right. That doesn't follow at all. It doesn't follow in any setting. If you and I were on the street and had an agreement, you would go to law and not to attack me on the street, just because I wasn't doing what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought you might say that, Sir Rupert, but you're the soldier and I'm the lawyer. Soldiers don't behave like lawyers, do they? Live in the real world is what I'd suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should join the real world discover --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness please slow down for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- Mr. Josse and General Smith, please, get back to question and answer, please, and avoid such -- such interludes, however entertaining they might be. But your next question. And slow down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you just repeat why you say I need to live in the real world because the interpreter interrupted understandably because we were both going too fast.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because soldiers have to operate within the law as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since UNPROFOR were unable to do anything about the demilitarisation of the enclave or were unprepared to do anything about it, what options were open to the VRS? Lawful options, of course.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, they had every opportunity to continue the blockade of -- the military blockade as opposed to the humanitarian blockade of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you accept, don't you, that weapons were being smuggled in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that that in itself was a possibility, not a very easy thing to do, when you've got lorries full of food, buried somewhere within the lorries are contraband weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to have happened at least once, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, at least once, yes. Let's have a quick look at 6D179, please. This is a Muslim document. We'll have the English up in a moment, I'm sure, but to help it comes from a Dr. Esad Hadzic who describes himself as the 2nd Corps assistant commander for intelligence, and it's to the command of the 28th Division. And it's dated the 26th of June of 1995 and it says, "In the morning hours of 26 June 1995, our forces attacked from the Srebrenica area and set fire to the village of Visnjica. According to as yet undetermined information, the Chetniks had casualties among the civilian population." Were you aware of that attack?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that specific specificity, but I remember that towards the end of June, there was at least one, if not more, attacks out from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And didn't it become inevitable at that point in time that the VRS would take military action to stop their civilians being massacred in this manner?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inevitable, no. That it didn't surprise me that there then followed a series of operations and indeed you've already seen documents with me saying that I'm expecting this to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 1D19 again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was a document I showed you in part yesterday from Brigadier General Jasarevic to General Delic, and it was what I described -- summarised as the February 1996 report by Jasarevic into the events at Srebrenica. It's page 5 in the English translation that I am interested in. And repeat yet again, it's important to bear in mind that this is a Muslim document. It's page 6 in the B/C/S original. About a third of the way down the page in English, "At the time of the Chetniks attack on Zepa on 9 July 1995, about 6.500 people lived in this area. They and members of the 285th Brigade were well supplied with all types of foodstuffs. In addition, information gathered to date indicates that cooperation between the civilian and military authorities of Zepa and the Ukrainian battalion which was deployed in the Zepa sector was good to the beginning of the Chetnik offensive. "After the commander of this UNPROFOR battalion crossed over to the command of the Chetnik forces, the new Ukrainian Battalion commander handed over all the weapons at his disposal to our soldiers. These were immediately used to defend Zepa. According to several displaced persons from Zepa, he even sent false reports to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo saying that members of the Ukrainian Battalion had been directly attacked and requesting NATO air strikes against the Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "he" in this case being the new Ukrainian Battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be how I read the document. That's correct. My question is were you aware of any of the matters described either here or in the documents we were looking at a few moments ago in private session?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of the attack on the Ukrainian position. Whether I knew of that that night or subsequently, I don't recall. The -- and by the time I got to the pocket myself, the subsequent dates, and we'd have to remind me of the dates, but we are about five days later, Ukrainian forces are certainly all muddled up with -- they are down in Zepa but they are also up the hill with Bosnian Serb forces. They were all standing around together. But none of this, as described there, is -- was known to me in the sense that it's described there and all of that is new news.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the allegations that the VRS had attacked the Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? Not -- no, I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the implication of this document.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that as a -- that the Ukrainians were attacked, no, by VRS. I don't remember that as a specific set of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been candid that allegations and counterallegations were a continual of a problem, and for UNPROFOR to discern who was telling the truth, when and how so to speak, was not an easy task to perform. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst we are on this particular document, we can see in the next paragraph a description of the fact that the Chetnik attacks on Zepa were commanded by an officer called Krstic and then supervised directly by the criminal Mladic. I asked you about that yesterday and you agreed with that. And then later on, after it deals with the name of some of the Bosniak negotiators, Torlak. Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Homanovic [phoen] and Kulavac [phoen], whom you've already referred to in your evidence earlier, it says, "The criminal Mladic and the Chetnik General Zdravko Tolimir represented the Chetniks at the negotiation." It's an obvious point but there is no mention of General Gvero, is there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir Rupert, I've been through this in some detail really to see whether it jogs your memory as to what your state of knowledge was in London at that time, and then the following day when you returned back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I returned on the 23rd, not the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember that the -- that Zepa was still going on during the London Conference. The problem was how to -- was quite clearly one at that time, as we've discussed already, which was getting the people out and there was -- and the Bosnian authorities were as concerned with this as anything else. The -- and my memory is that my understanding while in London of the -- that here was the evidence that this was a deal as I'd understood when just before we left for London Mladic, had shown me the first of those agreements, was that this was agreement with the civil population as opposed to one with the fighters, and this was more evidence of there being a split, if you like, within the enclave, as to who was in what group doing what thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And specifically in relation to these terrorist-type threats issued by the Bosniak defenders, you have a vague recollection, would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can remember those threats being issued. I'm not sure that I'm taking them quite as seriously as they're being written.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Hence presumably your comment that you'll only return if the massacre actually takes place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think I think at the time that -- that the Silajdzic and co. can control this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Palic we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nonetheless, it does appear on the evidence that the defenders did attack the Ukrainian base and did seize the weaponry. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that it had happened. Whether I knew it at that time, and immediately after it happened, I don't know. I can't recall the actual reporting sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you categorise the threats that we've just been through as terrorist-type threats?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would call -- I didn't categorise them like that. They were -- they were just threats. I wasn't in the business of being any more, you know, putting things in boxes at the time. This was a threat to try and get us to do something that I couldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our perception of the word "terrorist" has changed, has it not, since that time, as a result of the blowing up of the twin towers as much as anything else, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Globally we probably changed our perception of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You'll recall the document I showed you earlier. I put it back on the screen again, the Muslim document describing the attack in June 1995 on civilians outside of the Srebrenica enclave from the defenders of the enclave. Would you categorise that type of attack as a terrorist attack?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I was cat -- if I had to sit down and do a generic, if this is the question you're asking me, if a generic categorisation of terrorism, is that what you want me to give you a definition of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: An act that is intended to cause a political result rather than a military one by a -- an armed act or a threat of armed action, that is primarily caused to create a political effect rather than a military effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can agree, can't we, that word, both in 1995 and more particularly subsequently, is bandied around by politicians and sometimes by soldiers quite widely in a wider context?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the word is used extremely loosely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You will recall that I -- well, soon after I began yesterday, I asked you about member mementoes and gifts and it's that subject I'd like to return to now. In particular I'd like to show you two pieces of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we've done here is as follows. We have got the originals of these mementoes, for want of a better word, in Court. We've also had them photographed because we are aware that if we surrender the originals they will remain in the archives of the Tribunal, and we don't particularly want that to happen. And the photographs I think will suffice for the purposes of the actual exhibit which the Chamber will retain in due course. So let's see if this works. Could we start with 6D194, please, In e-court, which is a photograph, I hope. Yes. Let the witness have a look at the original. Madam Usher. It's a bottle of whiskey. It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not empty.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh!

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My client is obviously quite abstemious. It purports to be a presentation to Lieutenant General Milan Gvero from Major Wilcox, Chief of Staff of the Ace Rapid Reaction Corps, which is the name I think you couldn't remember before?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it's the ARRC. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you categorise a bottle of whiskey as more than a regimental plaque?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly not a regimental plaque, but it contains a great deal more use, but it contains essentially the same information on the front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I think you explained that you personally were not in the habit of giving something like this to the warring parties, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember doing anything of the sort, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think to be fair that this was in --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. It's dated the 4th of May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. So the war was at an end and that may be a significant factor. But you wouldn't do anything of the sort and --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That isn't to say I might have done such a thing. I don't recall doing it, and I don't recall having a supply of whiskey in bottles, for example, to give out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Let's have a look at the very thing that you had described earlier, which is a plaque which is 6D193. If you'd swap them over, please, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Bench are welcome to smell the whiskey and examine the label.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that General Gvero will ever have that bottle back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this in fact is the back of the plaque on the photograph. And we can see it's like a good military address, Ainsbury and Wiltshire [phoen], isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see it says at the back, to General Gvero, Michael Walker 13th of August 1996, Han Pijesak co-mark, and if we turn it next picture, please, in e-court, next page, I'm told in e-court, will show the front of the plaque. "Allied Command Europe Rapid Reaction Corps presented by Lieutenant General Sir Michael Walker." So we've got the whiskey in May and this in August of 1996. And in fairness to my client, I believe that Lieutenant General Walker is a highly respected British soldier. He went on to become Chief of Defence Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Was he chief? Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact he was subsequently ennobled and is Lord Walker of Aldringham; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I have nothing else. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. May I have confirmation first that there is no other Defence team that wishes to cross-examine General Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I certainly don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone who wishes to -- no, we hear none. One moment. Re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to show you a couple of documents and this will address some questions that Mr. Josse had for you, and I will need the assistance of Madam Usher. This was an area he just brought up towards the end of his examination. I want to show you a sit-rep dated the 16th and 17th of July. The relevant portion will be from the 16th of July. And if we could -- it's not in e-court. If we could just scroll up just a little bit, or just push it, there we go. General, you can see there it's the 16th and 17th of July, and we're at the 16th of July for the purposes of that middle column. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we slowly scroll down, do you see the numerous entries for UKRBAT, that's the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is a column of times on the left. Now, if we could kindly turn the page, please, Madam Usher? Do you see the entry at 19.55 hours? It's the very last entry coming from the Ukrainian company in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbs arrived to check-point 2, grid reference 481654 and threatened the Ukrainian company personnel that they will shoot them in case that the NATO aircraft strikes over the BSA positions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just put another document. I'll identify these for the record by the ERNs in a moment. It's a sit-rep dated the 16th of July. And if we could move it up just a little bit, I'm sorry, scroll down, please. There is an entry under Charlie. Would you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the high-lit bits or the whole of Charlie.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you could start with the first line, please. "Re-establishment..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just finding it easier for the -- "Re-establishment to communications between base and check-point 2, 481654, reported. The personnel of this check-point mounted defence. The Serbs directed their weapons to Ukrainian soldiers. The Serbs," re -- I'll -- reiterated spelt wrong, "That if NATO undertakes any actions against them, they will kill check-point personnel."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. I think that's it for the ELMO for the moment. And for the record, this second document was R 043-4743. And we'll give it the 65 ter number of 2959 for the record. The first document is ERN 0365-4126 to 4127. And that will be P02958 for the record. Now, if we may have 65 ter 2340 E which will be the English and B, which will be the B/C/S, displayed, please? General, while we are waiting for the B/C/S, this is an intercept taken by Muslim army intercept operators of VRS channels on the 16th of July, and we can see there at 1731 hours is the time that they have intercepted this conversation. If we could scroll down on the English a little bit, please, as well? There is a reference first of all to the boss, the boss received it, "Call the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo up there if you can, and tell them that we'll destroy UNPROFOR forces here in Zepa if they engage in air strike." And towards the bottom you see there is a reference, there is a statement, "Threatened them that we'll shell them as we did." General, do you recall whether this order to communicate this threat to kill UNPROFOR forces by the VRS was communicated to you in Sarajevo? Do you have a recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that being -- this incident, I don't recall it at all, or the threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may have 65 ter 528 on e-court, please, and we'll be looking at page 51 to begin with. And again we are just going to be looking at a couple of things in connection with something that Mr. Josse brought up today. You remember some questions he had based on an ABiH document about the raid on the 26th of June, it's the village of Visnjica; you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to talk a little about some of the activities that were going on earlier in the months. If we look at paragraph 223 we will have to scroll up to the top please, there we go. We are talking about the right-hand corner. It says, "In June 1995, the period of relative military inactivity came to an end. On 1 June a Serb raiding party entered the enclave ambushed and reportedly killed a number of Bosniak civilians. On the same day the BSA instructed UNPROFOR to move observation post Echo and UNPROFOR position on the southern boundary of the enclave," and then later on it says, "On 3 June the Serbs attacked the position with hand held weapons, mortars, and anti-tank weapons. General, do you recall the military activity beginning to pick up on or about the 1st of June, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all wrapped up in my memory with the May, the end of May bombings and the hostage taking. But I can remember that and the loss of the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please, to page 52, at paragraph 225, you see there is a description of the attack, "During the attack in the early morning of 26 June, several houses were burned and either two people were killed according to Bosniak sources or four according to the Serb sources. "The attack although relatively minor in comparison to the Serb attacks which preceded it led to strong Serb condemnations." There is a description of a protest by General Mladic, and then at the very end, "Mladic failed to mention what UNPF had reported to United Nations headquarters three days prior to the raid on Visnjica, namely, that the BSA had apparently fired 20 shells into Srebrenica town killing one woman and injuring another two civilians." General, do you remember these events as described here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you answer, General, yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Highly selective reading in my submission. The whole paragraph certainly got to be read by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: By all means, General, if you -- feel free to read the whole paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Smith, the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole 225?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To yourself, if you like, sure.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, just that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or any other paragraph you think might be relevant after having read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is still in early June. No, during -- this is late June, yeah. My memory of the whole of the period from May through to July was there was this -- these attacks and incidents going on. We were in -- we UNPROFOR were increasingly powerless because we had these people taken hostage. The use of air power had been withdrawn, the keys had been taken away from the military commanders. And we were -- and these events were happening. The precise order of them and so forth, I don't remember with any great clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were shown some of the demilitarisation agreements that had been entered into. I want to show you one document in connection with those. And with the Court's indulgence -- may we have 2951 on e-court, please? And if we could just scroll up just a little bit more on the English, please, little bit more. Just a tad more. There we go. Thank you. As you can see, this is a report or submission by Colonel Palic dated 9 July to the Armija General Staff, the 2nd Corps and 28th Division. He refers to it being the fifth day of the VRS attack on Zepa, civilians wounded, among two children, 30 houses destroyed. There is a specific reference here to: "If this situation continues, we have the approval of the commander of the Ukrainian unit to take back from them the weapons that we surrendered. Since we are a demilitarised zone, we ask for your views on this issue." You've already heard some references to demands for weapons from weapon collection points or otherwise. My question to you is simply: Would that be a violation of any of these agreements to agree to hand back the weapons to the Bosnians under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't remember the -- the basis of the original negotiations where that -- if that agreement existed, it would have been in there. The -- I have a better, slightly better memory of the weapon collection points that came into being when NATO declared these exclusion zones, and there, there was an understanding that they -- the weapons would all be collected. But if it was necessary to -- for them to be made available for self defence, then they could be. And that -- and that, if I recall it, was true of all the weapon collection points for both sides. Now, whether this is wrapped up in that or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked some questions yesterday by Madam Fauveau about when you knew what General Miletic's position was, and your answer at page 17621 was, "What I can't tell you is just how much I knew before I saw those documents and how much I'd forgotten and so forth." I want to show you a document, General, that I haven't shown to you before because we didn't have Rule 70 clearance when I met you for your proofing session. And this is 2952, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't object to the witness seeing and commenting on the document, but I'd like the answer to this document would be limited to the time when this document was written and this is completely outside the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your comments to, to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is not completely outside the time of the indictment, and I think we're entitled to show the document to General Smith and see how it refreshes or does not refresh his recollection as to what he knew about General Miletic's position during there period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed and then we regulate the questions and answers accordingly, if it is necessary, if it becomes necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the document, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we is see that that the date is 19 September 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's described as the notes from the meeting between Generals Smith, Bashale [phoen] and Generals Militic and Milosevic, and I don't think there is any disagreement that these are the more specific notes that were referred to in P02908 which was another document memorialising this meeting on the 19th of September, we've already talked about that. If we could go please to the second page of the document, the very first sentence states that "Following further discussions between the Holbrooke team and president Milosevic, another meeting was held between General Smith and Bashale and Generals Milosevic and Miletic (Miletic is Mladic's DCOS..." how do you read that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "And today was the first time we had seen him in the flesh.)" Does this refresh your recollection at all, General, as to what your knowledge was of General Miletic's position during the period in time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. What it tells me is that Baxter knew it, so if I'd asked him he'd have told me. That I can be sure but I -- I couldn't say that it improves my memory to any great degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the day before yesterday you were asked by Madam Fauveau, and this is at page 17624 of the transcript, "So you just said that the Armija and the VRS didn't have the same organisation, so is that correct that it is quite possible that there are significant differences in the importance of different positions in the two armies?" And your answer was: "I think it's probably fair to say that this is coloured by the personalities holding the positions rather than the positions as they stood in some organisational chart." And you were also asked if you agree that the organisation of western armies could be described as functional as opposed to the more linear organisations of the Soviet bloc. I just wanted to follow up very briefly on those two ideas that were put out to you. To what degree, if any, did the size of the VRS Main Staff from your observations and dealings with them affect how it operated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness answers, one should ask him if he really knows the size of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Taking into account Madam Fauveau's remark, or comment, or suggestion, General, can you answer Mr. Thayer's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- I was about to answer with another question, which is its size in comparison to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: In your experience and observations of the VRS Main Staff, can you describe whether -- actually let me ask you with respect to the VRS in general. From your observations and dealings with them, what was the -- the availability to it of an experienced officer corps?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding of what I was looking at and seeing and dealing with is that the Bosnian Serb army had a great deal more professional and trained officers than the other two, the Bosnian and the Federation armies. In comparison, they had a shortage of manpower. That would be the, I think, the primary difference between the two in answer to your question. I can go on expanding if you want me to but...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let me try to focus it a little bit. And based on your observations and interactions with the VRS Main Staff, in the context of your discussion of the capability and practice of the Main Staff to detach its forward commanders or its assistance commanders forward in the field, to what degree, if any, was that a product of the availability of high level commanders, specifically within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My objection is how does this arise? Now it's no question it doesn't arise from anything I asked. The question is whether it arises from anything that Madam Fauveau asked. I would suggest it doesn't. She cross-examined the witness about some general propositions to do with western and eastern armies. She was very careful to avoid this sort of specifics, and the original question in re-examination was perhaps permissible, but very quickly, my learned friend has strayed away from the areas that Madam Fauveau cross-examined upon, and it is extremely important, bearing in mind, I certainly made a decision not to cross-examine on this area, that the Court determine whether this is a proper line of re-examination. I submit it does not arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is also bound up in questions that may have had a generic sense to them but were clearly aimed at trying to identify or characterise General Miletic in a particular way. The questions about rank, about having commensurate rank at certain positions, were all clearly designed to focus on the role of her client. And if I may be permitted to put one portion of a meeting to the general, I think that the question will be precisely focused and that will be my last question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I firmly object to such a characterisation of things because when my colleague was asking questions that was part of the expert statement of this witness, it was clearly -- it was clearly meant to be linked to the accused here. However, I don't think it should be a basis to ask questions on the VRS and with the point of view that he speaks as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, I will be asking General Smith based on his observations how is what I would like to put to him consistent or inconsistent with his observations and that's as far as I wish to go, no expert testimony to be elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you go straight to the question? Dispensing of this one, because if it's -- it's supposedly a question that you're putting so that the next one becomes more clear, I think we can hear your question straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think you can frame it to incorporate what you had in mind in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we may be shown 2953, and we'll be looking at pages -- or page 35 of the English and 29 of the B/C/S, please. With the Court's indulgence. May we try page 44 and see if we have better luck, please, with the English, and page 37 of the B/C/S. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, these are -- this is a transcript of the minutes and tape recording of the 52nd session of the National Assembly of the Republika Srpska held on 6 August 1995. This is a portion of a statement made by General Tolimir on this occasion to the National Assembly. And if we look at the first full paragraph, it reads, "It has been said here that the General Staff was holding long meetings. I just want to say the following thing. We are the smallest General Staff in the world among all General Staffs either in peace or war, and all the officers of the General Staff are at the front. General Miletic is currently in the General Staff and it was always so. General Milosevic will not be left alone as he never was. "We are always sending someone from the General Staff and we are still doing it. There is a forward command post that is stronger than his command is and it is located in that part of the Sarajevo front. There are two forward command posts of the General Staff in his zone. We have been keeping General Milovanovic as the most experienced commanding officer as well as General Mladic. Pardon me," and that's Tolimir speaking. "Maric. At Grahovo Glamoc front and in line with a part of the Main Staff and the operations for four to five months, and I think that it cannot be accepted, being a member of the General Staff, I cannot accept this statement because we do not hold the meetings at all. We make expert analyses, we prepare directives, and based on those directives we all go in the field and work in accordance with the assignments that we receive. We carry out the assignments in accordance with our capabilities. Our manpower now is just -- I should not say the number. It might be a shame for me to say it and for other people to hear it since some journalists are present here." General, my question to you is having just heard that statement from General Tolimir, is that consistent or inconsistent with your personal observations of how the VRS Main Staff operated?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is broadly consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, it's happened now, but I'm going to mention that that is an outrageous leading question. To use a document like this which the witness has absolutely no connection with, never seen before, to ask a question is it consistent or inconsistent is not the way to conduct a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, if I may be permitted to follow-up given the answer we can find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was a direct question and re-examination you're still in the same position as you are when you are examining a witness in chief. And the practice here, throughout this trial, is that when there is an objection to the use of direct or leading questions, you avoid using them. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and keep that in mind please that you have a standing objection from Mr. Josse at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, when I asked you whether it was inconsistent or consistent your answer was it was broadly consistent. Can you be more specific as to what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is describing the establishment of these forward headquarters alongside subordinate headquarters and that they shift them from point of effort to point of effort, and there is a shortage of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
