utterances.text: And what is inconsistent in that statement with what your observations were of how the VRS Main Staff operated?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- and this may be in the terminology -- if he's referring to the Main Staff as just the main headquarters, then the inconsistency is that I understood and saw all their command arrangements as being part of the Main Staff as opposed to the main headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move on to another topic quickly, General. Madam Fauveau showed you an excerpt from the NIOD report concerning the level of medical supplies in Srebrenica in early April and you had some disagreement about whether what was being talked about in that section had to do with DutchBat medical supplies or the situation in Srebrenica itself and that was at page 17662 to 663 of the transcript. And she read to you a section which ended with the statement by the Dutch Minister of Defence having to do with the state of affairs on April 10th. I want to direct your attention to a section of NIOD just a couple of pages later in that same chapter, General, and this is at 2954. And if we could turn to the next page, please? And we will be focusing on the right-hand column, please. General, do you see the paragraph beginning with "The field dressing station treated"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You see it refers to the field dressing station treating a Bosnian woman for seven weeks in the months of April and May of 1995. And it goes on to describe why she was there. "The consumption of medical supplies required for her heavy demands on the stock." If we move down a little bit, "Since the hospital staff were unacquainted with this type of case and Medecins Sans Frontieres had almost run out of medical supplies, an appeal was made to the know how of DutchBat's surgical team. "The hospital had asked DutchBat for a second opinion on 5 April after which the patient was transferred to the compound in Potocari where she was stabilised and prepared for transport to Sarajevo. Although permission had already been granted for this transport, the Bosnian Serbs at Zvornik refused passage from the unit to the Norwegian medical detachment in Tuzla which was to fetch the woman. "Since the woman would die if she was not given medical treatment, DutchBat decided to continue to look after her. An entire team was needed for her intensive care which meant that the programme of humanitarian operations had to be completely stopped." Now, if we move down just a little bit in that paragraph, it states that the materials required for her treatments had been in short supply to start with and were soon exhausted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the benefits of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "The medicaments she needed then had to be smuggled in by convoys of DutchBat personnel returning from leave. Oxygen had to be made from atmospheric air and her nutrition had to be improvised. After six weeks treatment, however, the woman died of an internal -- of an intestinal infection which had affected many people in the compound from time to time. One of the things that had to be smuggled into the enclave for the woman's treatment was a particular type of muscle relaxant. The Norwegians in Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down because the accused are having problems with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "The Norwegians in Tuzla did not have it in stock, and so would not have been able to supply it even if they had been allowed access to the enclave." Now, if we just turn to the next page, please, and we will be focusing on the left side, "Since the woman's general health and her prognosis after Krdic [phoen] were good, intensive care was continued. However, as mentioned above, her care up to the time of her death made great demands on the medical supplies. Dopamine and intravenous antibiotics were completely used up, as were the drip feed supplies, though the pharmacist managed to make up a replacement mixture from tinned Protifar obtained by making an appeal to all body builders in DutchBat and peanut butter. General, did you ever hear in your command in Sarajevo about this case of this woman who was treated by DutchBat and the effects it had on their supply?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall being made aware that the DutchBat medical supplies in April had been depleted to the point described there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly knew they were short of medical supplies. That I knew. Along with other things. But the -- the degree, I don't recall how depleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a lot of questions about food resupply to the enclaves. Just briefly, what was your understanding as to how much or how little the civilian populations of Srebrenica and Zepa depended on the food and other supplies being delivered by UNHCR and other NGOs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is memory. They depended -- they needed the resupply, and particularly after the winter. There was a capacity to -- there was a certain capacity within the pockets to feed themselves and so forth, but a -- but extra food particularly the bulk things like flour and so forth was necessary. I can't remember the exact quantities or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, in answer to one question, you said that the DutchBat soldiers, when you visited them in March, certainly weren't starving. And I want to show you a sector Sarajevo report from June 3rd. That's 2956, please. And there is the cover page, General, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of the document, just want to briefly draw your attention to one paragraph, it's at the bottom. It's headed "Zepa Supply Crisis UN Soldiers cut Down Their Rations." "The supply situation in Zepa has reached a critical point. There have been no fuel convoys to Zepa since 7 March which compelled the Ukrainian company there to stop running generators. "Consequently, refrigerators are not suitable for food storage. Since 23 May the company is on dry rations which will last only for a few days. The soldiers are cutting down their rations consuming only two meals per day. The problem of resupply convoys for Zepa should be urgently addressed at the highest level." My question, General, is do you recall receiving this report of the situation of the Ukrainian soldiers in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that specific report, no. But I know that as I've said, the -- after May, particularly, the situation was getting more and more difficult in those -- in those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may be shown 2497, please? Now, General, do you still have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can see that this is a document dated 18 June 1995 from the VRS Main Staff. Regarding the approval of certain UNPROFOR convoys. If we look at paragraph 1, do you see the reference to a convoy whose destination is Zepa on 20 June?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the cargo is a container with dry and fresh food, eight tonnes, one container with ten tonnes of water, and one ten tonnes cistern with fuel, and I don't think there is any dispute that the signatory on this, just to save some time, is then Colonel now General Miletic. Now, if we could look at another Sarajevo sector situation report, 2957, and we'll link up these two documents, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to answer my colleague, I don't contest the fact that my client's name is on this document. However, I challenge the fact that he did write it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dated 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's sector Sarajevo weekly situation report. If we could go to the fifth page of the document, please, and we will be focusing on the bottom paragraph. "After 16 weeks without fuel convoy and after having run out of food altogether, the Ukrainian company in Zepa finally received a resupply convoy this week. The convoy reportedly carried 525 kilograms of ketchup," and I won't go into the rest, but it says, "It did not include any meat, salt, sugar, flour, oil, pasta, et cetera, et cetera." General, had you heard that the Ukrainians had run out of food?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this incident, no. Or that they had actually run out of food by the end of -- of this -- this is late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You saw the previous document listing the tonnage of cargo. Had you heard reports of shipments, UNPROFOR resupply shipments, arriving without their cargo or with only portions of the cargo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- by this stage in June, these convoys are with I think only one exception, all run out of Zagreb through Serbia, and I -- and there were cases where, I think, if I remember rightly, where what was supposed to arrive didn't arrive, and this would appear to be one of them. But I don't know -- I think we thought this was -- in Sarajevo I think we thought this was a failure of organisation in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at another document and that's 2496. This is a communication from commander Major Rajko Kusic. Does that name mean anything to you, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. It's dated the 23rd of June 1995, attention of the Main Staff, General Mladic. It refers to document 06/18-249, 18 June 1995, and that's the first document we looked at in this series.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Refers to the ten tonnes of oil which were approved to pass through together with other provisions. And then goes on to state that "We are informing you that in agreement with the commander of the Ukrainian units we have taken five tonnes, that is half of the authorised quantity for the needs of our brigade." General were you aware of any such agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And had you heard in the past of VRS demands for half or a portion of the fuel?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, those had been put to me at some stage, I think as -- in either March or April. Yes, I think it was April probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you regard such demands?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they should -- you know, I wasn't interested in falling in with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why not, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was fuel for my people, not for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back in time just a little bit, and we'll be finishing up shortly. I may need a couple of minutes after the break, Mr. President, but we are nearing the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 2531. General, we can see that this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, it's dated 10 March 1995. First line says, "we hereby inform you that we have approved the following UNPROFOR convoys." Do you see at paragraph 1 there is a reference to a convoy to Zepa on 11 March?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, there is a note, "we did not allow the transport of 30 litres of electrolyte, tires, 24 volt headlights, 20 spark plugs, 4 break cylinders, 1 battery and 1 transmission set for an armoured vehicle." If we could go to page 3 of the document, please, and this is going to be the second page of the B/C/S. Do you see the note at the top of the page regarding the items that were not allowed on the convoy for Gorazde, fruit, butter, honey, ham, drinks. The next paragraph 4 refers to a convoy to Srebrenica on 11 March. Do you see the note where it says, "we did not allow the following, three tankers and five trailer trucks"? And if we look at the very bottom of the page, please, "we did not allow 36 cubic metres of diesel fuel, ten crates of dry food, frozen food, cold food, and there is other materials and spare parts," and so forth?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page to page 4 of the English, and this is still on page 2 of the B/C/S, under paragraph 5, again there is a note, "Did not allow the transport of 15 gas cylinders." Paragraph 6, the bottom of paragraph 6, "We are talking about in addition to these requests, the following requests were submitted for which we did not grant them our permission." And the first item is a convoy to Zepa consisting of, among other things, one fuel tanker, and then on item 2 there, another fuel tanker, and if we turn the page in English, we'll see that that was supposed to transport petrol to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just if you can read 3, 4, 5 to yourself you'll see there are other references to fuel, tankers, diesel, petrol, oil, not being permitted.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the other documents we showed indicated foodstuffs being called for but then not arriving at the destination. Here we have a document which indicates that certain things were not permitted to begin with. Was that reported to you, General, that there were certain items that were prohibited or things that were not approved at all into the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, not in the detail of this document, but the general restriction on the free supply of the contingents in the enclaves was -- I was aware of that fairly early on and certainly by March. All of that was part of why I started to think the thoughts I thought and arrived at what I've called the thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just have one more question on this document, General, and then we'll have to take the break. If we could go to the next page of this English document, and that will be the last page of the B/C/S, page 3 of the B/C/S. And we'll have to scroll all the way down on the English, please. Do you see where it states, "Discuss the information on unapproved convoys with check-points, do not tell third persons, and do not give any explanations to UNPROFOR representatives (Pretend that you did not get them.) If a convoy shows up at a crossing points, return it to the place of departure." And if we turn the next page of the English we will see who the signatory is on this. And you can see it on the B/C/S, do you see who that is, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's Miletic, General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, did you have reports of convoys just simply being turned back without explanation? Do you recall those incidents?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- certainly convoys and a convoy could be just one or two vehicles wanting to go and visit somebody, not getting through a check-point. I don't remember, and the end of that document, I don't remember a specific case of a convoy that had been cleared being stopped. That doesn't come to mind. But that you didn't have freedom of movement, that I was definitely a problem from pretty well the -- as soon as I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just have one more document, and then I'll be done with my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, just one more document. The last one we looked at was dated the 10th of March, and you testified about a 5 March meeting you had with General Mladic in which you concluded or from which you concluded that a high level meeting had just occurred. I think you testified about observations of Mr. Stanley and your own personal observations, and then you also spoke about a meeting in Vlasenica with General Mladic in which you described how he would shrink the boundaries of the enclaves and why he was imposing certain restrictions. If we may see P5 on in e-court and if we could go to page 2 in the English. And I'm pretty sure that's going to be page 1 of the B/C/S. Yes. We have a document headed directive for further operations number 7. And its date is 8 March 1995. General, I just want to draw your attention to a couple of sections in this document. If we could go to page 10 of the English and that's page 15 of the B/C/S, please. If we could scroll down on the English, please, and the B/C/S is good where it is. A little bit more to the bottom of the English. Thank you. Under the paragraph headed "Drina Corps," I just want to draw your attention to the section that reads, "While in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." General, based on your meetings with General Mladic and your observations and your development of your thesis based on those observations, can you tell the Court how this section of the document either fits or doesn't fit, support, doesn't support, your thesis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer, General, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see to what part of the cross-examination this question refers to or flows from. It is my colleague from the Prosecution who spoke of the various meetings during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I certainly support that objection and invite my learned friend to identify how it arises, but I make the same objection that I made earlier that this is really a leading question. If the witness was an expert, then I could see my learned friend being allowed to put this document in front of him and asking him that question. But bearing in mind he's a fact-based witness, to put this assertion in front of the witness and then ask him to comment upon it is leading in a direct, not a veiled form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we heard extensive cross-examination of General Smith about the justifications for actions taken by the VRS, by motivations of the VRS for taking actions that they took, for the -- with respect to the timing of certain events that occurred and the motivation for certain things that happened at certain times. I am asking General Smith for again based on his experience, his observations, the development of his thesis, based on those personal observations, whether what he is reading here, whether it is consistent, inconsistent, supports, or doesn't support, what he was seeing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position, having discussed amongst ourselves, Mr. Thayer, is that the excerpt from this document that you read out to General Smith doesn't really require his opinion on it or whether it tallies or doesn't tally with what he has stated here on oath to be his position on the events on the ground at the time. So we don't think that the question is necessary in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so I understand, when Mr. President you say his position, you mean including his factual observations? And if that's the case, then I'll that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's told us what his factual observations were. He spent days at length here telling us that. It's true that he's been contested by both Mr. Josse and Madam Fauveau on some of his observations, but what's this going to change? I mean, it's a document which speaks for itself and which doesn't really need anyone to explain it, except maybe the person who drew it up or knew more than General Smith knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In that case, General, I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I be allowed to ask some further questions to the witness on two documents that my learned friend from the Prosecution has shown to the witness during his questions? It will take only five minutes. One of the questions will have to do with the NIOD report excerpt. I believe three lines from that excerpt have not been read by my learned friend and I believe they should be because they are significant, and the other question will have to do with a document dated the 10th of March on convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, Madam Fauveau. Further cross-examination by Ms. Fauveau:

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P2954? Could we move to page 2, at the very bottom of this page, on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, my learned friend read most of this portion, but he did not read what starts on this page and ends at the next page. The portion I'd like to read to you is the following: "[In English] The Americans had limited supplies of this muscle relaxant but stated that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "They were only prepared to provide it if it was required for DutchBat and not for the general population. Charleton [phoen] had replied that he needed it for a member of DutchBat personnel but still use it for the woman." [Interpretation] On the bases of these two sentences it appears these medicines did reach the enclave and it was used in order to treat that woman, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what that appears to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to have a look at document P2531. Could we see the date of this document, please? It is a document on the passage of convoys. This document is dated 10th of March 1995, a few days after you met General Mladic; is that correct? Where General told you that he was going to restrict the passage of convoys headed towards the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. We have got some questions for you, General. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Sir Rupert, I just wanted to take you back briefly to the encounter that you described with General Gvero at Zepa, at the check-point. And in your direct testimony you in summary spoke of a conversation that you had with him at that time. I take it that conversation must have been through or with the use of an interpreter or interpreters, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would have had one with me. As I say, either Captain Bliss or Captain Dibbs, but I'm pretty sure that must have been how it had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: But you don't have any specific recollection of the conversation and who was interpreting it for you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any memory of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And in terms of the conversation itself and the content of it, would you say that your recollection is as clear of that as it is of the fact that you encountered General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The memory is of the meeting him in those circumstances and that he said that he was now in charge. Why I asked him how that came about and so forth, other than that we had met, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost. Sir Rupert, we have come to the end of your testimony. You were scheduled to return on the 23rd of this month but I don't think there is need for that. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I would like to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we go through this, Prosecution exhibits? We have a whole list here. I haven't counted them. Any objections, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid there are two objections, particularly to the third entry on the second page, where my learned friend seems to be trying to get the whole of the expert statement of July 2006 into evidence. These are my observations, that if there are passages which he says that he in effect took as read, because let me stop there I accept that he conducted his examination in a way that sensibly assumed the Court had read the document because we know the Court had read the document prior to its previous ruling. If there are passages which fit in with the expertise permitted by the Trial Chamber's order and/or by observation of the witness, then I'm quite prepared to look at those and consider whether they should be admitted into evidence. They need to be identified clearly, and frankly we need to be given a little bit of time then to consider whether we accept the admission of those passages, but the admission of the whole document I oppose vigorously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do think there is a basis for admitting the entire document at this point. As Mr. Josse has said, at the very least, the section concerning the importance history function of a Main Staff which is approximately the first ten pages of the document is separate from the rest in which he is being shown various VRS documents for the most part. The Defence questioned General Smith on the issue of you never said in your witness statement such and such about my client. And I think it's important for the Court to be able to, in order to judge whether that is fair or accurate or give whatever weight to that assessment, the Court should have access to the entire document. I think we can trust the Court, given the Court's clear order, of what is permissible for consideration in terms of his fact versus his expert testimony. I think to be efficient, it just makes sense for the whole document to go in, particularly with all the references to western versus Soviet model armies, many, many topics which are dealt with in the expert statement were addressed, and given where Defence counsel went in some of its examination, it's important for the Court to be able to at least see and read the entire document and give those portions that are dealing with his examination, for example, of certain VRS documents, whatever weight the Court deems appropriate given the Court's clear order that we, I think, tried very hard to abide by with General Smith's testimony. I think to try to redact it or chop it is not going to be possible, frankly, given the way some of the examination was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I don't think we need to discuss this much further but Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully support the objection raised by my colleague from the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Madam. I need of course to confer with my colleagues, yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind Your Honour's comments. I won't respond to what Mr. Thayer said. There is one other objection, perhaps I could deal with that now. That's 2953 which are the five pages in English, seven in the original, from the National Assembly minutes of the 6th of August 1995. The one page that was put to the witness, I won't object to, although it was read out in full. The rest of it I see no reason why it should go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My friend is entirely correct. I cut down the examination. So we are really talking about only the first entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now the entire document is in e-court should there be a need to refer to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, are you in a position to identify the first entry? I think it's the one pages 35 to 45 or just one page, 4296. Someone needs to identify exactly the first -- the page that you made use of. I think you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. President, if I might add, Richard Butler, for example, will be talking about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But let's leave that. All I'm saying is that since you agree that it's only this excerpt that needs to go into the record as an exhibit, it needs to be identified. As regards the other one, I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The position is as follows, Mr. Josse, Mr. Thayer, and Madam Fauveau, for the time being, we will mark document 6D00183 for identification purposes, limitedly for a period of a week. That's until today week, by which time, Mr. Josse, you need to indicate to the Trial Chamber or detail your objection in relation to parts. It doesn't mean to say that we are agreeing beforehand that we will eventually admit this statement, witness statement, with redactions. It doesn't mean -- by no means saying that, but we are giving you the opportunity to explain yourself better by reference to the parts that you object to and then we will take a decision. After one week, obviously, the statement will be admitted with or without redactions depending on what we decide. Depending on what we decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the onus is on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The onus is on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can do it of course together with Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to file this and with an argument, Your Honour? Or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The argument you have made. What we are interested in knowing is which parts specifically you are referring to and objecting to. That's all. The argument he has made already. He's saying if this document is to be admitted, it has to be admitted into conformity with our previous decision that there should be no inclusion in it of any expert opinion on matters that we decided he was not to be an expert witness upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's right and the submission is that weight doesn't really come into it, unless the Trial Chamber are going to admit it for a very specific purpose; for example, the one that Mr. Thayer raised in relation to my cross-examination on non-mention of Gvero. But I personally see no need for that but if it's going to be admitted on a very limited basis at least we would know where we stand, but I understand the ball is in our court to say which parts we specifically object to in accordance with the previous decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And is a week enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would rather have two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes. You will have two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the -- no objections in relation to the other documents? So all the other documents will be admitted. There are -- there is one at least that will be MFI'd, that's the intercept, in accordance with our previous decisions. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to let the Chamber know that we have no objections to either tender sheet submitted by either Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And to be precise, at least for the record, I have a list from the Miletic Defence team and I have a list from the Gvero Defence team which you have all seen. No objections from the Prosecution. Are there any objections from any of the Defence teams? The other Defence teams? None. So these documents are also admitted. However, I notice that there are a few that are still awaiting translation and until that arrives, they will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar will identify them. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, the very last entry in our list, we didn't have a number for. I don't know whether Madam Registrar can assist. We need to assign it. Apparently we will do that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Akashi report. We have got barely 15 minutes left if you want to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly not beyond 2.00, and I need the okay from the staff. I can't see behind the dark glasses, check for me, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We shouldn't take too much time, Mr. President, but this is just to report to you on your order or suggestion that we get together with the Defence and try to work out some of the timing and logistic issues related to especially the 98 bis issues. We've done that. And we have some agreements which I will try to go over, and I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong on anything. These are of course suggestions to the Trial Chamber as -- from us on ideas that we agreed to would be appropriate. We agreed that 98 bis submissions would occur one week after the close of the Prosecution's case. We agreed that each Defence team would have one and a half hours to argue and that they could time share with each other if they found that others would take more than one and a half hours; that the Prosecution would have up to two days, if needed, to respond; that both sides could supplement their oral submissions with written submissions of a reasonable length and identification, simple identifications of areas of fact and law. The item we disagreed with was on who should go first. The Prosecution would like it if the Defence would go first so that we could respond to their arguments that thereby hopefully limiting our time to what the Defence brings up, and as I had mentioned to the Trial Chamber before, we would appreciate any guidance on any particular issues the Trial Chamber would like us to address. And of course, the Defence would like the Prosecution to go first. There is also a somewhat related logistical area that everyone agreed the importance of Serbian Orthodox Christmas, and -- which is 7 January. There are no flights from Belgrade on 8 January. So Defence counsel from Belgrade would be flying back 9 January. So 10 January everyone agreed would be an appropriate start date, which would be in accordance with, we were here, as you recall, last Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also on the 9th we will be engaged with the exchange of new years greetings with Her Majesty here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So everyone is fine on that and I believe the Defence will address you on the amount of time they would like between the end of the Prosecution's case and the beginning of their case, and the Prosecution stands neutral on that point and would leave that up to the Trial Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. Who is going to be the "spokesman," quote unquote, for the Defence teams on what Mr. Haynes -- Mr. McCloskey has just mentioned? Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll be the spokesman insofar as it relates to confirming the discussion we had yesterday. I wouldn't go as far as saying we had a disagreement as to who should go first. We are really in your hands as to which procedure you think would be more helpful, and it did seem to us that the suggestion from the Prosecution that there would be forms of skeleton argument in which they wanted to identify relevant areas of law and fact tended to point towards them going first rather than us. And I would also just mention, in that regard, that if you look at the amount of time that this procedure might take, in our view, it would take less time for there to be one speech from the Prosecution, seven in response from the Defence, and maybe one reply from the Prosecution than it would the other way around which would make for 15 separate speeches. But we are not going to fall out about that. We had a very open and good discussion. And we are in your hands as to what you think is the best procedure to adopt. The collective view of the Defence is that a break after the determination of the 98 bis arguments of three months would be appropriate and necessary, and I'm perhaps the worst to argue this point sitting as I do at number 7 in the indictment, and so, as it were, the white heat of starting my case is not perhaps as great as it is for, for example, for Mr. Zivanovic. We believe that a greater period at the conclusion of the 98 bis proceedings and before the commencement of the Defence cases would make for greater economy of time in the long run, because it would enable us to filter and edit our cases, to prepare more evidence to be admitted to the Court through Rule 92, whether it be bis or ter. And so on and so forth. There are also a number of cooperative expert issues which are some way from being ready to be filed at the moment. We understand the pressure of time that the Trial Chamber is under but that is our request. And I will put it no higher than that. We are of course in your hands. Is there anything else I can help you with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just let me check whether we have covered everything, Mr. Haynes. I think that covers practically everything that we had discussed as well. Yes, Mr. McCloskey? I'm sorry, I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more point. Mr. Nicholls provided me with something that we are tending to guide ourselves by in this, and you may recognise the words from the Oric case, where you, I believe, said, that "we do not wish to hear any submissions by you in particular trying to explain why you believe that you have proved your case with a 98 bis standard for each and every area. If an area is contested to you by the Defence, then do so by all means. You will respond and try to contest and make submissions." I won't go on. But that is something that we are guiding our 98 bis submissions by and if that's still appropriate, we intend to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, precisely. I think we direct you to what the rule says. Basically, reading through that rule, you should know what the exercise ought to be. I think it's pretty straightforward. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that covers all except for two things. We already had a hint from you during very short exchange on this a few days ago on whether, who should go first, whether it's the Prosecution or Defence. We have discussed it amongst ourselves and our position is that the Defence should go first. We are not going to intervene or interfere as to who should go first amongst yourselves, and I think we can safely say that you can also agree amongst yourselves to make use of any disposable leftover time that remains, accepting that you will have an hour and a half each. We'll come back to you on another point that was mentioned by Mr. McCloskey, whether you would be allowed or asked to supplement with -- you mentioned two things, submissions as well, indicators both as regards fact also as regards law. We'll come back to you on that. We have discussed that amongst ourselves as well, but we'll come to a decision later on. Paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's enough for today. And we'll also confirm to you that we'll respect as we did last year the Orthodox Christmas but that's to be confirmed. That's to be confirmed later. Which would mean basically that we would start in January on the 10th and not on the 7th. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
